Key bindings are desktop settings

Status: accepted. Settings contract 0.4.0 (additive). Widens Desktop settings have one native ABP authority, whose scope was the desktop's appearance and layout.

Context

Every egui application offers its actions as commands with optional shortcuts (egui applications). Before this decision each application kept its key bindings its own way:

  • dopus read an overlay file, keymap.conf.mix, in its config directory, once at start-up;
  • ced had a fixed table of Notepad++-style defaults;
  • BusViewer and Preferences had shortcuts written into their command lists;
  • each parsed chord text in its own way (ArrowLeft in dopus, Left in ced).

So a person changing a key had to know which application kept it where, an agent could not change one over the Bus, and nothing could show every binding in one place.

Decision

  1. The user's bindings live in settingsd. The authored desktop profile gains keymaps: per application id, per action id, the list of chords the person chose. An empty list unbinds the action. An action that is not listed keeps the application's default.
  2. Defaults stay with the application. An application's default chords ship in its code, beside the actions they run, so a new action arrives with its key and an application without settingsd still has its keys. settingsd stores only what the person changed.
  3. One chord grammar. A chord is modifiers then one key, joined by +: Ctrl, Alt and Shift, in any order, then a key name. Key names are egui's (ArrowLeft, PageDown, F6, Delete, Num1), a single letter or digit, or one of the short forms Up, Down, Left, Right, =, - and /. Ctrl is the platform's command key. One stroke per chord. settingsd checks the grammar; the application checks the key name, and reports and skips one it does not know.
  4. Edited by the existing transaction. settings.apply takes keymaps.<app> (the whole map, or null to drop every change for that application) and keymaps.<app>.<action> (a list of chords, or null to return that action to its default). Limits: 16 applications, 256 actions each, 4 chords per action, 32 bytes per chord.
  5. Followed live. The summary (settings.get {view: summary} and the summary topic) carries keymaps, omitted while empty. Each application applies its own entry whenever the profile's revision changes, so a new binding works at once, without a restart.
  6. How an application applies them. The toolkit's command registry keeps the defaults it was built with. Applying a profile entry starts from them:
    • each listed action takes exactly its listed chords: the first is its menu accelerator, the rest also run it;
    • a chord the person bound takes precedence over a default, and the default loses that chord;
    • an unknown action or key is skipped and reported in the application's log.
  7. The record format is unchanged. keymaps is authored and omitted while empty, so every stored profile re-serialises byte for byte and its seal still verifies. It has no effect on the resolved design, so the effective digest and design revision do not move when only a binding changes.

Consequences

  • dopus no longer reads keymap.conf.mix. No such file existed on the running session, so nothing needed migrating.
  • <app>.commands reports each command's effective shortcut and its further chords, so an agent can read what a key does before and after a change.
  • A shell that decodes the full snapshot (deny_unknown_fields) must be rebuilt before a profile carries keymaps. The portal is one; it is rebuilt with this change.
  • A Keyboard Shortcuts page in Preferences can follow: it reads each application's commands over the Bus and writes keymaps.<app>.<action>.

Not covered

  • The compositor's own bindings (workspace and window keys) are not an application's commands; they stay in the compositor for now.
  • Multi-stroke chords, and keys an editor widget handles itself (Cut, Copy, Paste and the cursor keys in ced's editor).
